'''Gary Paul Nabhan''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|n|æ|b|h|æ|n}}; born 1952) is an agricultural ecologist, [[ethnobotanist]], [[Order of Ecumenical Franciscans|Ecumenical Franciscan Brother]],<ref name="wholeterrain.com">{{Cite web |url=http://wholeterrain.com/2015/10/metamorphosis-author-profile-gary-paul-nabhan/ |title=Bock, C.Metamorphosis author profile: Gary Paul Nabhan, 6th paragraph, Whole Terrain, Franciscan Action Network, October 5, 2015 |access-date=January 10, 2016 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304042848/http://wholeterrain.com/2015/10/metamorphosis-author-profile-gary-paul-nabhan/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="divinity.wfu.edu">{{Cite web |url=http://divinity.wfu.edu/archived-ecotones-2015/speakers/gary-paul-nabhan/ |title=Wake Forest University School of Divinity |access-date=2016-01-10 |archive-date=2016-02-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160207162122/http://divinity.wfu.edu/archived-ecotones-2015/speakers/gary-paul-nabhan/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> and author whose work has focused primarily on the plants and cultures of the desert [[Southwestern United States|Southwest]]. He is considered a pioneer in the local food movement and the heirloom seed saving movement.

==Background==
Nabhan is the grandson of [[Lebanese Americans|Lebanese]] and [[Syrian Americans|Syrian]] refugees. He was raised in [[Gary, Indiana]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=webmaster |title=Ethnobotanist Gary Paul Nabhan on embracing the 'wisdom of the desert' |url=https://www.garynabhan.com/news/2022/08/ethnobotanist-gary-paul-nabhan-on-embracing-the-wisdom-of-the-desert/ |access-date=2023-12-22 |website=Gary Nabhan |date=31 August 2022 |language=en-US|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003144900/https://www.garynabhan.com/news/2022/08/ethnobotanist-gary-paul-nabhan-on-embracing-the-wisdom-of-the-desert/|archive-date=October 3, 2022|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=webmaster |title=An Interview with Author Gary Paul Nabhan |url=https://www.garynabhan.com/news/2023/12/an-interview-with-author-gary-paul-nabhan/ |access-date=2023-12-22 |website=Gary Nabhan |date=December 2, 2023 |language=en-US|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231209073947/https://www.garynabhan.com/news/2023/12/an-interview-with-author-gary-paul-nabhan/|archive-date=December 9, 2023|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=July 2019 |title=The Canary Islands Connection |url=https://www.aramcoworld.com/articles/2019/the-canary-islands-connection}}</ref> He excelled at [[William A. Wirt High School]],<ref>{{cite news|last=Kiesling|first=Donna|date=May 12, 2002|title=Getting down to nature|url=https://www.nwitimes.com/uncategorized/getting-down-to-nature/article_90c1a753-5a97-5ff1-a80e-7d37c83d249f.html|url-access=subscription|work=The Times of Northwest Indiana|access-date=December 8, 2025}}</ref> which gave him the opportunity to attend [[Cornell College]] in [[Mount Vernon, Iowa]], for 18 months. He then transferred to [[Prescott College]] in [[Prescott, Arizona]], earning a B.A. in Environmental Biology in 1974, and has remained in-state ever since. He has an M.S. in plant sciences (horticulture) from the [[University of Arizona]] (1978) and a Ph.D. in the interdisciplinary arid lands resource sciences also from the University of Arizona ("Papago Fields: Arid Lands Ethnobotany and Agricultural Ecology," 1983).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.azarchivesonline.org/xtf/view?docId=ead/uoa/UAMS337.xml;query=;brand=default|title=Gary Nabhan papers1978-1995 (Bulk 1969-2008) Nabhan (Gary) papers}}</ref>  During this time, he started working with, and learning from, the [[Tohono Oʼodham]] American Indians.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Gary Paul Nabhan, Ph.D. | url=http://www.garynabhan.com/press/Nabhan%20long%20CV%202008.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081121004635/http://garynabhan.com/press/Nabhan%20long%20CV%202008.pdf | archive-date=2008-11-21}}</ref>

He co-founded [[Native Seeds/SEARCH]] while working at the University of Arizona. It is a non-profit conservation organization which works to preserve [[endemic (ecology)|indigenous]] southwestern agricultural plants as well as knowledge of their uses (1982–1993). He then served as director of science at the [[Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum]] (1993–2000), before becoming founding director of the Center for Sustainable Environments at [[Northern Arizona University]] in Flagstaff, AZ (2000–2008). In 2008 he moved back south to Tucson and joined the [[University of Arizona]] faculty as a research social scientist with the Southwest Center, where he now serves as the Kellogg Endowed Chair in Southwestern Borderlands Food and Water Security. He sits on several boards of conservation organizations.

As detailed in his writings, he married at a young age and had a family, but he was divorced in the late 1980s, later marrying a second time, this time with Caroline Wilson in the early 1990s. He is currently married to his third wife, Laurie Monti (formerly of Northern Arizona University) and lives near [[Patagonia, Arizona]] on a five-acre homestead to the southwest of town.<ref name="garynabhan.com">{{Cite web |url=http://garynabhan.com/i/archives/806 |title=Our Farm : Gary Nabhan |access-date=2014-01-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140202105848/http://garynabhan.com/i/archives/806 |archive-date=2014-02-02 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He farms a diverse set of heirloom fruit and nut varieties from the Spanish Mission era and from the Middle Eastern homelands of his Lebanese ancestors, as well as heritage grains and beans adapted to arid climates.<ref name="garynabhan.com"/>

==Contributions==
The unifying theme of Nabhan's work is how to avert the impoverishment and endangerment of ecological and cultural relationships, while celebrating the traditional ecological knowledge of the agrarian communities. He has played a catalytic role in the multicultural, collaborative conservation movement, being one of the co-authors of its populist manifesto, "An Invitation to the Radical Center."<ref name=Nabhan>Nabhan, Gary Paul, and 19 others (February 2003).  "[https://web.archive.org/web/20170331185224/http://quiviracoalition.org/Community/An_Invitation_to_the_Radical_Center/index.html An Invitation to the Radical Center]".  Quivara Coalition website.  Retrieved 15 April 2017.</ref>
Nabhan was among the first creative non-fiction writers to link the loss of [[biodiversity]] to the loss of cultural diversity. In his book with Stephen Trimble, ''The Geography of Childhood'', he was among the first popular writers to show concern with the loss of children's access to the natural world. He has been a significant contributor in calling attention to the environmental issue of [[pollinator decline]]. He founded the Forgotten Pollinators Campaign, the Migratory Pollinators Conservation Initiative, and attempts to restore nectar corridors for pollinators in bi-national watersheds around his home in [[Patagonia, Arizona]], which he calls the "pollinator diversity capitol of the United States."

In addition to the articles and books on pollination ecology for which he has been sole author or editor, he co-authored with Stephen L. Buchmann one of the key works on the topic ''The Forgotten Pollinators'' from [[Island Press]] (1996).

He is a champion of [[rainwater harvesting]], which he implements in his own orchard and gardens, and he has written introductions on this topic in permaculture books by Bill Mollison and Brad Lancaster.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BCVZPWmFyqAC&q=permaculture+bill+mollison+brad+lancaster&pg=PA222|title=Harvest the Rain|date=2010 |publisher=Sunstone Press|isbn=978-1-61139-114-5|pages=222|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Hemenway|first=Toby|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gxW0MGXha6cC&q=permaculture+bill+mollison+brad+lancaster&pg=PR11|title=Gaia's Garden: A Guide to Home-Scale Permaculture, 2nd Edition|year=2009|publisher=Chelsea Green Publishing|isbn=978-1-60358-223-0|pages=xi|language=en}}</ref>
